analysis.one_liner: Exempts offshore export companies from tax rules and lets them convert to tax-advantaged export subsidiaries.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have cut taxes for offshore export corporations and their shareholders, was introduced with no cosponsors, never left the Ways and Means Committee, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite tax rules for export trade corporations (ETCs) and foreign sales corporations (FSCs) — offshore subsidiaries US companies use to route export sales through and reduce their tax bill. It would exempt these entities from the "passive foreign investment company" rules, which were written to stop Americans from using foreign entities to defer tax. It would also repeal the rules that currently tax ETC income to shareholders each year, treat distributions made since 1984 as already-taxed money, and let ETCs convert to FSC status without recognizing any gain on the transfer. The practical effect is that owners of export vehicles would pay less federal tax; the cost would be forgone Treasury revenue. The bill never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders and owners of export trade corporations and foreign sales corporations — in practice, large US exporters that route export income through these offshore subsidiaries. The bill would free them from the passive foreign investment company rules, ending the risk that their export vehicles would be taxed like punitive foreign investment funds, and it would wipe out the rules that currently tax shareholders each year on the vehicles' earnings. Converting an ETC to an FSC would also be tax-free.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the definition of a passive foreign investment company so that export trade corporations and foreign sales corporations are never swept into those rules, retroactive to the 1986 tax reform that created them.

Repeals the export trade corporation rules that currently tax shareholders on the corporation's export income as it is earned, and treats distributions made in years after 1984 as previously taxed income, so shareholders would not owe tax on those payouts.

Lets any export trade corporation elect foreign sales corporation status for years after 1990, with no gain or loss recognized when the corporation transfers property into the new entity — a tax-free conversion.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would collect less tax, since the bill removes rules that currently tax export corporation income to shareholders and exempts those entities from anti-deferral rules. General taxpayers bear that cost through higher deficits or offsetting taxes.

drawbacks.text: The passive foreign investment company rules exist to prevent Americans from using foreign entities to shelter income from current tax; carving out export vehicles would preserve exactly that deferral opportunity for a favored category of corporate shareholders.

The bill reduces federal revenue at the same time the government was running large budget deficits, and the benefit would go to a narrow group of export businesses and their owners rather than to ordinary taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had a plausible housekeeping rationale: Congress had replaced the older export corporation regime with foreign sales corporations in 1984, so clarifying the transition and confirming FSCs were not caught by the passive-investment rules had some logic. But the substance is a tax cut for a narrow set of export corporations and their shareholders, paid for by the Treasury. The export tax preferences at issue were the same ones international trade partners later challenged as export subsidies, so the bill would have deepened a contested and ultimately unstable subsidy rather than reform it. The costs are real; the benefits reach a small, already-advantaged group.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 1990, referred to the Ways and Means Committee the same day, and the committee took no recorded action before the Congress ended in early January 1991.

narrative.text: Representative Robert Matsui introduced the bill on September 28, 1990, near the end of the 101st Congress.
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means that same day; no markup, hearing, or floor action followed.
No other member cosponsored the bill.
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, the existing rules that tax export corporation income to its shareholders stayed on the books, and the Treasury kept that revenue. Export companies and their shareholders did not get the exemption they sought.

for.name: Rep. Robert Matsui
for.role: Sponsor; member of the Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured its referral to Ways and Means, where he served.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; took no recorded action after the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for markup or a vote, leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no opposition was recorded; the only visible support was a single Democratic sponsor with no cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Export trade corporations and foreign sales corporations
industries.note: These offshore subsidiaries exist mainly to reduce US tax on export income. The bill would exempt them from anti-deferral rules and wipe out rules that currently tax their earnings to shareholders, letting them keep more income tax-free.

industries.industry: Large US exporters (aircraft, machinery, agriculture, pharmaceuticals)
industries.note: Big exporters use FSCs and ETCs to cut the tax on foreign sales; the FSC regime functioned as a tax subsidy for exports. The bill would expand and lock in that benefit, with the revenue cost spread across all taxpayers.
